audit: The delivery analogy warns that a timeout cannot establish non-delivery, but readers need to weigh contradictory observations rather than simply memorize a recovery slogan. Lesson A supplies a timed-out shipment call, an authoritative shipment lookup and a missing fee result, separating observed effects from unresolved ones. Lesson B follows a persisted refund intent through same-key recovery and a prohibited replacement identity. The downstream dedupe record, retention window and unchanged payload are explicit. Neither the local ledger nor a new worker is treated as sufficient for uniqueness, and the examples preserve uncertainty so that compensation or replacement cannot outrun reconciliation of the original operation.

lessons.title: Which parcel actually exists?
lessons.intro: A replacement saga recorded inventory, shipment and fee intents. The shipment response timed out. Recovery now has three observations; decide which conclusions each can establish.

claims.text: The shipment timeout proves no parcel was created.
The fee charge definitely failed before taking effect.

sources.text: Carrier lookup for OP-S91: succeeded; shipment S-91; status prepared.
Client event: shipment response deadline elapsed after request submission.
Fee journal: OP-F91 intent saved; no result or authoritative lookup yet.

data.verdict: Shipment exists; fee outcome unknown. Reconcile before choosing recovery.

read: The carrier lookup is evidence of a shipment effect despite the lost response.
The timeout alone describes the caller's waiting outcome.
The incomplete fee journal leaves its external effect unresolved.
lessons.question: Should recovery cancel the shipment solely because no fee result is recorded?
lessons.answer: No. First establish whether the fee took effect. If it succeeded, cancellation may leave a charged customer without the replacement. The saga must choose compensation from known outcomes and preserve unresolved obligations.
lessons.takeaway: Reconcile effects before deciding what to compensate.
lessons.assumption: Fictional saga; carrier lookup is authoritative for OP-S91. Absence of a local result does not establish absence of an effect.

lessons.anchor: Idempotency keys and duplicate side effects
lessons.title: The same refund must reach the same remote record
lessons.intro: OP-61 was persisted before payment submission. The provider committed refund R-61, then the worker crashed before saving success. Recovery occurs 5 minutes later within a documented 24-hour dedupe window.

edges.label: Atomic dedupe returns original result R-61

read: The absent local success record is the crash gap.
The permitted recovery retains the exact operation identity and payload.
The downstream atomic mapping supplies duplicate protection inside its retention contract.
lessons.question: What changes if recovery occurs after the provider has discarded OP-61?
lessons.answer: The shown same-key guarantee no longer applies. Recovery must use a supported authoritative reconciliation path or escalate before any resubmission. Retaining the local intent cannot recreate an expired downstream dedupe record.
lessons.takeaway: Match the recovery horizon to downstream dedupe retention.
lessons.assumption: Fictional provider contract; current authorization checks remain required. Routes represent enforced policy, not guarantees created by this drawing.
